I'm hearing several rumors that frontier labs have broken some major cryptographic primitives:

- "Factoring is in P": Now that the Riemann hypothesis is proven, we do understand much better how primes are distributed. Still, I don't think factoring is in P. 
AKS showed in 2002 that primality testing (deciding whether a number is prime) is in P, but factoring is a different beast. If it were in P, RSA would simply be broken, and that would be huge: a large part of our systems still rely on RSA.

- "ECC has been broken": Other rumors say elliptic-curve cryptography has been cryptanalyzed, which would take down ECDH and ECDSA along with it. (all the non-RSA asymmetric cryptography)

- Ring-LWE isn't quantum-resistant. That wouldn't be an immediate threat, since there's no cryptographically relevant quantum computer yet. But it would make the ongoing post-quantum migration pointless.

It's hard to tell what's true. AI has made incredible progress, starting with the proof of the Riemann hypothesis. 

And most importantly, if a frontier lab did find something like this, a clean responsible disclosure that avoids mass exploitation would be very hard to pull off. All of this helps the rumors spread.

Personally, I don't think findings like these are coming. I wouldn't be surprised if some of these primitives turn out to be a bit weaker than we thought, but I'd be very surprised to see any of them fall apart completely.

Releasing a new blog: Scaling Swarms to Thousands of Agents!

The biggest problems in science are tackled with huge swarms of agents, but the knowledge to run such swarms is hidden inside a handful of labs and missing from the wider community. Many questions remain open:

- How do even you launch 1000s of agents?
- What's the best form of collaboration?
- Which tools are needed for agents to work effectively?
- What breaks at this scale and how to fix it?

This blog is a fully open field report covering all the practical and technical challenges of running large scale swarms we experienced and which are usually missing from the reports.

Here are a few lessons we learned while building pybot with 1000 DeepSeek agents for over a week:

- achieve diversity without enforcing too much structure
- monitoring and steering a swarm as it runs
- early signs of misalignment, from infrastructure probing to trading review approvals
- breaking and fixing git 
- message boards and communicating at scale
- finding the bottlenecks: inference, tool calls and context compaction

Today we are also sharing two of our internal tools: legion and msgboard! 

Legion is a harness agnostic framework to spawn 1000s of agents on a variety of infra (local, slurm, hf jobs etc.)

Msgboard is a simple message board you can run locally or on a space, and allows agents and humans to collaborate.

Read the full report here: https://t.co/8Y4HJ1vUtt

tweets.content:
Yes, actually a bunch of them. Apart from efficiency gains, self-coordination among agents, in a swarm  increases coverage by a lot.

For e.g, I published a benchmark last month (https://t.co/8r4RbFKNZh) where I compared models from all leading labs (including open-weight models) against an application containing 60+ complex vulnerabilities. Back then, none of the open-weight models performed well, and they were far behind frontier models.

Over the last few weeks, I have been tweaking different combinations of swarms, some inspired by nature (like how ants, bees, bird flocks & fish schools coordinate) and some very simple ones using an append only message board. 

i observed that, by using only open-weight models in a self-coordinated swarm with a shared message board where they collaborate (and using the combinations I mentioned above), while also letting some agents work blindly (because n agents starting with the same prompt will produce n different results), I was able to achieve near-frontier-level recall on some tasks. The coordination among them acted as a multiplier for the vulnerabilities they discover, and it was 2x-5x result sometimes in terms of no of vulns discovered.

Apps like Spotify, Discord, Reddit, Substack, and Wise all do quiet research on you. These trackers link you across ad networks and/or analyze your behaviour in their apps.

A good chunk of the cybersecurity industry exists because of insecure code, insecure defaults, and decades of technical debt.

Models should be generating secure code by default, not double dipping on tokens to go back and secure the code they just generated.

Much of what we deal with today stems from legacy systems and backwards compatibility. Windows is a prime example of the security challenges that come with decades of supporting legacy functionality.

If we’re heading towards a world where it costs more to secure software than the value that software delivers, there’s a fundamental economic imbalance.

The goal should be to reduce the cost of security through better engineering, not turn security into a bigger industry than the thing it’s protecting.

tweets.content:
Someone who read the deck told me this was the most important slide for them, because they hear the same thing all the time: the attackers use AI, so the defenders should just use AI too.

If they attack us with fire, why not defend with fire? Because you can burn yourself.

The asymmetry isn't in the technology. It's in what a mistake costs. An attacker's agent can pick the wrong exploit, look at the error and try another route. It only needs one to work. Once a defender's agent is allowed to isolate hosts, kill processes or disable accounts, every wrong call can become a production incident, even when no attacker is there.

That doesn't mean AI has no place in defense. It can move fast where a mistake is cheap: correlating telemetry, rebuilding timelines, collecting evidence, searching other systems for the same traces. A wrong guess there costs an unnecessary query. For actions that change production, I'd keep the agent that reasons apart from the component that is allowed to act, and decide in advance which actions are safe enough to run on their own.

I think automated response will come, first where the consequences are clear. Until then, the attack surface has to shrink.

I wrote about this in more detail in August:
https://t.co/F3ciMHYJlP

Agentic Offensive Frameworks have cost me a few nights of sleep over the last three months.

I'm convinced we're entering a new era in cybersecurity, and to be honest, it frightens me. I expect a lot of friction and some havoc, and I'm not sure how many organizations can withstand it.

The way I see it, the internet as we know it only worked because nobody had the time to look closely at most of it. Every system got scanned, but almost nothing got a careful second look. #AOFs remove that limit. Now everything gets that look. And I don't just mean source code, vulnerabilities and exploits. The whole threat landscape shifts.

So I kept asking myself what this means for the future, and for the things we build tomorrow. I came up with a term for my answer: defensive minimalism. 
I think it's the way forward.

In the post I explain what I see as the core problems, and why I think tomorrow will look very different from today in many ways.

RT @olegkutkov: This is how it works: a Raspberry Pi 4 combined with a few components from the original Starlink router hardware.

V1 - Gen 1 — router_gen_1
V2 - Gen 2 — router_gen_2
V3 - Gen 3 — router_gen_3
V4 - Mini integrated router — router_mini_cohoused_1
V5 - Mini router — router_mini_1
V6 - MINI2 integrated router — router_mini_cohoused_2
V7 - Gen 4 — router_gen_4

The firmware files itself is just a tarball with bl2 image, kernel fip and openwrt root squashfs.

Rootfs contains the network configuration for the USB Ethernet dongles and Linux kernel includes USB Ethernet drivers for chips I specified in the previous post.

Fire Point's ballistic program encompasses two missiles built for distinct roles — tactical and strategic.

FP-7 is Fire Point's first ballistic missile. RT @oegerikus: We’ve raised over $270 million for @Xbow.
3 pieces of advice I’d give to every founder:

1. The partner matters more than the fund.

You are not working with the entire VC fund. You are working with one person for many years, so choose the right one.

I'’ve been lucky to have @Konstantine  from day zero, and then @apoorv03, @rsayar and @SanjotMalhi. Each brings a unique perspective that helps me run the company better.

2. Know what the money buys before you raise.

Before you raise, know exactly where you will spend it. For us it buys speed. XBOW is growing at a furious pace in a competitive market, and the funding lets us hire the best people and build the product faster. It also helps us stay ahead of attackers who already leverage AI to find exploits.

3. Only raise when you have a clear plan for the money.

Raising a round is not a requirement for success. My first company, Semmle, grew organically over 13 years before GitHub acquired it. The pace was slow and deliberate, and we got away with raising very little.

I’m sure others have different advice, I’d be curious to hear it.
